title: Version one
hookLine: gather your pages into one short rule: Sariputta begs the Buddha to lay down rules, and the Buddha says wait
tomorrow: a man swore to do the basics, no more, no less. was that enough?

cards: A new notebook, and the urge to write the perfect plan before living a single day of it. The Buddha's disciple Sariputta had a version of that urge.
At a place called Verañja, he asks the Buddha: why did the teaching of some Buddhas of the past last a long time, while others faded?
Because some laid down training rules for their followers, the Buddha says, and some didn't. Then lay them down now, Sariputta says. He isn't being fussy; he wants the teaching to last.
And here's the odd part. The Buddha says: wait.

teach.h: WAIT: THE TEACHER KNOWS THE TIME.
teach.b: Wait, Sariputta. The Teacher will know the time. A rule isn't laid down until the trouble it's for actually shows up in the community.
In the Vinaya's telling, that's how the Buddhist monastic code grew.
Not as a manual written in advance, but one case at a time.
Something happens, someone is harmed or confused, it's brought to the Buddha, and a rule is made, with the story often kept beside it.
That's why the Vinaya reads partly like a book of stories: a training rule usually comes with its origin. The Patimokkha, the list monks and nuns recite together, is the gathered result.
It wasn't drafted in a quiet room; it was collected from life. Here's the teaching, named plainly: in Buddhism, a rule answers real life.

It's built from what actually happened, then refined as more happens. A rule of your own can grow the same way. You've already written the pages: the body, the people, study, the breaking rule, the season.
Version one doesn't invent a new life. It gathers what months of practice already showed you, and puts it on one page. The perfect version can wait.
The real one starts from what's there.

how: The Buddhist monastic code, the Vinaya, records each training rule with the case that led to it; the gathered rules, the Patimokkha, are recited by monks and nuns on observance days. A personal rule of life is often drafted the same way: from what has actually been kept.

games.q: your new roommate writes forty house rules before move-in day, for problems that haven't happened. what would the Verañja story suggest?
o: start with a few, and add rules as real problems show up, the way the Vinaya grew.
write every possible rule now; that's how the Buddha's code was made.
skip rules altogether; the Buddha thought communities didn't need them.
games.why: the Buddha told Sariputta to wait: a training rule comes when the trouble it answers appears. The code grew one case at a time.

practice: Gather your pages: the body, the people, study, the breaking rule, the season. On one fresh sheet, by hand, write the line from each page you've actually kept, not the one you wish you'd kept.
If a page has nothing kept, leave its line blank; that tells you something too. Then sit with the page on your lap for the rest of the time.
